paper: Beth A. Bechky, 2020 (Administrative Science Quarterly, Vol. 65(3), pp. 606–643; the copyright line prints 2019)

readings.wager: The one change of practice the paper records was written down before the comparison with DNA reached the unit. A plan for estimating measurement uncertainty was a requirement of the laboratory standard the lab was adopting for accreditation, and toxicology already held one, set to run three years. Read from here, practice at MCCL moves when a body with a hold on the lab or on a test has issued a written rule: the accrediting association and state law in toxicology, the scientific working group in narcotics. The DNA benchmark, which the paper itself calls an 'informal standard' with no rule-making behind it, gave the toxicology change a date and a name. If read this way, the evidence supports a narrower claim than the one at this place: a technology's standing can hurry, and lend its vocabulary to, a change that a formal standard already required of a neighboring occupation. It does not show the benchmark by itself reshaping the work of people who do not use the technology.

evidence.job: Says the lab was moving to ISO 17025 before the NAS report, that the standard required a three-year plan on measurement uncertainty, and that the unit had the plan when it heard of the challenge and chose to carry it out at once. Places the content of the change in a written standard and leaves the challenge the timing. The plan is clearly dated before the challenge; that it also predates the report is implied by the order of the sentences, not stated outright.

Defines DNA profiling as an 'informal standard': a yardstick used in the field for comparison, with no formal rule issued by the state or by professional associations. The reading turns the paper's own definition on the toxicology case, where a formal standard was in play.

Says the accrediting association was already asking the lab to meet this one standard on measurement error, and that state law and the association already set the confidence level for blood-alcohol results (p. 627); the discussion adds that changes already under way for accreditation made it easier to respond (p. 635). The reading promotes the written rule from a help to the main cause.

Prints a toxicologist telling the criminal justice community that the lab was not scrambling because of the NAS report, and citing scientific and standards documents for uncertainty of measurement. No toxicologist's printed words mention DNA; the link to DNA is made in the author's voice, through what the defense attorney was expected to argue (p. 627). The unit's own account of the change names standards, not the benchmark.

Reports that the NAS report barely mentions toxicology and does not criticize it, and that a defense attorney was winning [6 words of Bechky (2020), p. 625] attacking reports that left out uncertainty estimates. Shows the demand arriving as a legal campaign about measurement; the reading wagers that the campaign did not need the DNA comparison to work.

Narcotics practice already follows the working group's written guideline of two crystal tests in different solvents (p. 630), and a veteran analyst expects the unit will have to give up crystal tests if they are disallowed (p. 631). A second unit where bench practice tracks a written rule, and where a comparison with no rule behind it had changed nothing yet.

In Table 2 the professional-association entry is a set of accreditation standards for toxicology, a debate for narcotics and nothing for firearms, and only toxicology is recorded as adapting. The paper's own summary lines the one change up with the one written standard.

what_it_would_take_to_cohere.observation: The three-year plan as written (when it began, when it was due, what it required reports to state), set beside the first report or testimony that carried an uncertainty figure and beside the defense challenge as it was actually made. If what was implemented is what the plan already specified, only sooner, and the challenge was argued from measurement standards, the reading holds. If the form of the change (for instance the move from a 95-percent level to a stated range at 99 percent, pp. 627–628) was set by the challenge and its parallel to DNA, the paper's reading holds. The paper prints that the plan existed and what the new report could state; it does not print the plan's text or dates, or any words of the attorney.

strains_against.why: The laboratory directors' association answered the NAS report by promoting accreditation of all laboratories. The formal standard and the DNA benchmark are then not two separate sources: the benchmark may have been working through the rule, which the reading treats as independent of it.

The paper traces the challenge to the NAS report's conclusions being taken up by DUI defense attorneys and says the attorney meant to compare the lab's practice with error measurement in DNA profiling; the toxicologist's own phrase, that uncertainty is not just spurred by the report, concedes the report a part. If so the benchmark made the deadline, and a plan to apply procedures over three years might never have put a figure in every report without it.

Firearms examiners say their documentation changed over time, and the paper names no written rule behind that change. If there was none, practice in this lab has moved without a formal standard, against the pattern the reading claims.

With no rule yet in force, narcotics analysts were already worried, debating review requirements and pricing microscope cameras. A benchmark with no rule behind it had set a unit's agenda, which is more than supplying words, and the paper explains their holding on by values, not by the absence of a rule.

readings.who_could_complete_it: Whoever kept the lab's accreditation file in those years, such as a quality manager or a toxicology supervisor; or the documents themselves: the dated three-year plan, correspondence with the accrediting association, the defense filing or transcript in the DUI case, and blood-alcohol reports from before and after.

readings.wager: The narcotics unit did not turn the benchmark down; it could not afford the one way of meeting it that the paper counts as change. The law in its jurisdiction sets a short clock on drug cases, the unit has two instruments, and a crystal test takes minutes where an instrument run takes far longer. A veteran analyst herself states what the crystal test lacks, an output that someone else can check later, and the unit weighs cheaper ways of supplying one, such as cameras on the microscopes. What the analysts refuse is making the instrument their first method, and the reasons the paper prints first are hours and machines. Read this way, talk of autonomy and variety is how a capacity limit is defended, not what holds the line. The evidence would then support a different limit on the claim at this place: a neighboring occupation's answer to a benchmark is bounded first by throughput fixed in law and equipment, and the 'compatible' technique the paper enters for narcotics is an instrument that could not carry the caseload.

evidence.job: Gives the legal clock (charges depend on what the drug is and how much, so results are needed fast), the 10 to 15 minutes a crystal test takes for the most common drug, and the fact that the unit already runs GC/MS on unknowns. Sets the constraint, and shows the question is the mix of methods, not the taking up of a new one.

A veteran analyst states the crystal test's weakness herself (no written output, nothing for others to review later), expects the unit will [6 words of Bechky (2020), p. 631] instrument, and objects that this takes much longer and delays results. Shows the benchmark's test conceded and the cost counted in time.

A second analyst, speaking of a workshop on a court hearing that challenged crystal testing, says the county's caseload could not be kept up without crystals, with only two instruments and long runs. States the limit as a number of machines, and gives capacity as the answer even to a court challenge.

Analysts object to second-analyst review because it would double the time per case, and discuss microscope cameras as costly but far cheaper than more instruments. Shows the unit ranking ways of producing a checkable record by cost, and open to the one that leaves turnaround alone.

Analysts time themselves on typical cases and press an IT representative over a filing system that slowed each one; the paper says they valued efficiency because of the turnaround requirement. Shows speed as a standing concern of the unit, set from outside, apart from the debate over technique.

The findings heading lists quick identification among the unit's values (p. 630), but the summary table and the discussion keep only variety, autonomy and craft judgment (pp. 633, 637); the same table calls narcotics technique compatible on the strength of one 'infrequently used' instrumented analysis. Marks where speed drops out of the paper's account, and the reading takes the infrequent use as the finding: compatible in kind, not at the volume the jurisdiction requires.

what_it_would_take_to_cohere.observation: Whether analysts of the same training keep crystal tests where throughput does not force the choice: a controlled-substances unit with instruments to spare and no statutory clock, or this unit after cameras or more instruments were paid for. If such analysts still choose crystals and speak of variety, values hold the line as the paper says; if the mix of methods follows capacity, the reading holds. The paper reports a day spent observing the controlled-substances unit of an Eastern county laboratory (p. 614), in the region where the instrument is the first choice (p. 628), but prints nothing seen there, and it prints no later outcome at MCCL.

strains_against.why: The paper says what troubled analysts most was losing autonomy, variety and control, and prints two of them saying so in terms of judgment, training and boredom, with no mention of time. On their own account more instruments would not change their minds, and the discussion rests its case for values on exactly this.

Several analysts had earlier left toxicology to get away from routine instrument work. The taste for variety had already moved careers, apart from any question of capacity, so it is hard to treat as only a way of speaking.

The paper itself treats efficiency as something the analysts value because of the turnaround rule. It can therefore absorb the capacity story into its account of values; the reading needs a line between constraint and value that the paper does not draw.

The camera idea is one sentence of discussion with no purchase or trial reported, the review option is argued against and not costed neutrally, and the same veteran calls the crystal test very definitive. The evidence that the unit conceded the benchmark's test and was looking for a way to pass it is thin.

readings.who_could_complete_it: An analyst or supervisor from a drug unit that runs the instrument first, or from this unit in later years; and records that set capacity against choice: instrument counts and run times, caseload and turnaround figures, equipment requests, and the method used per case before and after any new equipment.

readings.wager: The passage names what the toxicologists did only as interaction and action 'around change', set off by a challenge that had not yet been made. The findings give that action a shape: a statistical write-up prepared for one court case, a new figure in the report, and a public session in which the unit tells the legal community that it was not scrambling, that it was already doing this, and that its instrument and method were what they had been for five years. Read this way, the unit answered the comparison by saying it was not answering one. It worked up a figure from records it already kept, in the terms the coming cross-examination would use, and presented the result as continuity. The three conditions in the claim then explain something narrower than a change in local practice: how quickly a unit can re-present its existing work to an audience it expects to face. 'Fit' becomes partly a position the unit takes in public, not only a fact about its technique. The evidence would support a claim about what toxicology says in court, and not yet one about how it analyzes blood.

evidence.job: The passage itself: the challenge is called potential, and the outcome is described as interaction and action around change, with no statement of what was changed. In the text the challenge is still to come (pp. 625, 627), though Table 2 (p. 633) and the summary given for this place speak of direct challenge or exposure. Sets the response as one made to an expected audience and leaves its content to the findings.
Says the unit put its statistical analysis together in order to testify in the pending case. Ties the first product of the change to a court date.

In an [7 words of Bechky (2020), p. 627] a toxicologist denies that the lab is scrambling because of the NAS report, says it was already doing this, and stresses the same instrument, an unchanged method and years of data already collected. The paper uses this to show compatibility; the reading takes the statement as the response itself, a claim of continuity made to the people who would challenge the unit.

The paper says the unit's reports did not yet include the standard (p. 627) and that results can now be stated with a range at a 99-percent level, where the lab had reported at 95 percent (p. 628); the toxicologist's 'already doing it' sits on the same page as the first. What changes in print is the stated figure, and the reading works in the gap between the two statements: new on paper, old in the telling.
Gives the bench routine for a blood-alcohol batch step by step, once, with no step marked as new or altered. As printed, the bench has no before and after.

Says DNA's own standing was built after court challenges through ways of presenting evidence, including statistical estimates and stated error, while its analysts still regard the bench work as messy and dependent on judgment. Suggests the benchmark is itself a way of presenting results, which a neighboring unit can meet by presenting.

what_it_would_take_to_cohere.observation: A dated before-and-after of the blood-alcohol routine, and of what the unit said in its own meetings when it decided to act. The reading holds if no step at the bench changed when the figure entered the report and if the unit, among its own members, spoke of readying an answer for the coming case while telling the legal community nothing had been rushed. It fails if steps were added or altered (controls, replicates, calibration, review), since the work would then have changed and not only its description. The paper prints the author's one-sentence summary of the decision (p. 627) and the public statement that instrument and method are unchanged (p. 628), which is the statement the reading treats as a claim; it prints no bench comparison across the change and no words from the unit's own meetings about the decision.

strains_against.why: The toxicologist describes working through the whole procedure, each piece of equipment and each reagent, to assess, quantify and combine their uncertainty. That is new analytic work on the method, more than a restatement of old records, even if the method itself stayed the same.

The paper describes writing reports and testifying to them as part of what forensic scientists regularly do. On that description a change in the report is a change in work practice, and the reading's line between account and work is one the paper does not draw.

The toxicologists talk excitedly about their reporting practices as new and are visibly proud of them. A unit that held nothing had changed would have less to be proud of; the pride fits the paper's account of a change embraced.

'Already doing it' can be read plainly: a three-year plan required by the laboratory standard did exist before the challenge. The statement may be an accurate report of preparation, as the paper takes it, and not a position struck for an audience.

readings.who_could_complete_it: A toxicologist or technical reviewer who worked in the unit on both sides of the change; or the unit's own paper trail: dated protocol versions, quality-control logs, notes of unit meetings, and a run of blood-alcohol reports and testimony from before and after.

readings.wager: Hold the occupation constant and read the firearms half of the passage again. The MCCL unit, whose testimony had met no challenge in its own courts, had still changed how it works: examiners say that claims to know a mark on sight no longer pass in reports or testimony and that judgments must now be backed with images, which the unit makes for the witness stand. The examiners at the statewide meeting who spoke from experience of contested testimony do not line up behind change in what the paper prints: one calls for it, others attack the critics, and nothing is known of what any of them altered at home. Read this way, the remote route does change local practice, slowly and through the occupation's own channels of training and expectation, and a local, dated challenge adds speed and visibility inside an 18-month window more than it adds force. The senior examiner's pride in never having been challenged is then as much a result of earlier change as a reason for none now. The evidence would support a contrast between two occupations in 2009 and 2010; it would not yet support a contrast between two kinds of route.

evidence.job: The passage and its note 5: MCCL examiners had met no challenge in court and did not treat colleagues' reports as their problem; [7 words of Bechky (2020), p. 635] at admissibility hearings seemed motivated to change; the author has no data on what those examiners did locally. This is the paper's one comparison of exposed and unexposed members of the same occupation, and the note marks where it stops.

Examiners report that their practice changed over time: claims to know a mark on sight no longer pass, and judgments must be backed with images. The unit images every set of marks for use on the stand, and a second examiner follows and signs each step. Shows a change of local practice, aimed at testimony, in the unit the paper records as resisting change.

An experienced examiner says outsiders have reviewed his work [6 words of Bechky (2020), p. 621], and the paper says the unit's [6 words of Bechky (2020), p. 624] its jurisdiction. Suggests the earlier change did not follow a challenge to these examiners' own testimony, and supplies the pride the passage cites.

At the statewide meeting some examiners answer the attacks by going after the critics, one of them saying that testifying has become harder since the report; another, questioned in court by defense attorneys and not barred, calls for attention to bias and more convincing testimony. In the findings, experience of contested testimony goes with defensiveness as well as with reform; the discussion's summary on p. 635 keeps only the reform.

All three qualified examiners are trained in the striae-counting method, one says he turns to it in borderline cases, and they recognize its appeal to outsiders. Shows the quantifying method already inside local practice as an occasional tool, again with no local challenge behind it.

Firearms examiners train for a year in a statewide program and a further year in the lab, studying manufacture and many images of close non-matching pairs. Shows a channel through which field-wide expectations reach a local unit with no courtroom in between.
Fieldwork ran from February 2009 to August 2010, with [7 words of Bechky (2020), p. 614]. Sets the window inside which no change in firearms was observed.

what_it_would_take_to_cohere.observation: What the firearms examiners who had been through admissibility hearings changed at their own benches afterwards, set beside what the MCCL unit had already changed, and when and on what occasion it did so. If the challenged labs moved further or faster on the same points, or MCCL's own move to images followed a local event, the local route adds force and the claim holds. If their practice matches MCCL's, or MCCL changed first with no local occasion, the reading holds. The paper says it has no data on the challenged examiners' local actions (note 5, p. 635) and gives no date or occasion for MCCL's earlier change (pp. 621–622).

strains_against.why: Inside the fieldwork window the MCCL examiners turned down the change the comparison actually asked for, numbers and counting rules, and the paper ties this to distance together with values and technique. An earlier change in documentation does not show that a remote demand touching judgment would ever move them.

The paper does not say what made claims of recognition on sight unacceptable. Technical review is done in every unit of the lab, so the cause may have been local and formal (lab rules, accreditation), in which case the earlier change says nothing about remote routes.

The one examiner the paper clearly shows being questioned in court about the legitimacy of his evidence is the one calling for change, which is what the claim predicts. The court experience of the defensive speakers is less clearly stated, so the split may not cut against exposure.

In toxicology the sequence fits the claim as stated: a plan that could have run for three years was carried out at once when a case arose in the lab's own jurisdiction. Whatever the firearms record shows, the local route visibly changed the timing there.

readings.who_could_complete_it: A firearms examiner or supervisor from a laboratory whose testimony went through an admissibility hearing, together with a long-serving member of the MCCL unit who can date its move to images; or dated documents from both: procedure manuals, older and newer note packets, training curricula and hearing transcripts.
